product.title: German 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 German: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how German builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. German is a close cousin of English — *Haus*, *Wasser*, *Hand*, *trinken* read themselves — so this course spends its time on the spots that actually trip English speakers up: der/die/das, the accusative, separable verbs, and a verb that insists on second place. They are taken apart one at a time, never all at once.

cover_design.label: GERMAN
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in German for complete beginners — from saying hello to telling the story of yesterday's trip.
cover_design.catatan: Every line of dialogue comes with a word-for-word translation and a pronunciation guide.

blocks.text: German has a reputation it doesn't quite deserve. People hear a word like *Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung* and decide the language is impossible — yet those long words are actually the easy part: just a few short words glued together without spaces. And as an English speaker you start with a head start: *Haus*, *Wasser*, *Hand*, *Finger*, *trinken*, *kommen* — German and English are close cousins.

What really holds beginners back lies elsewhere, and there is not much of it: every noun has a gender you have to learn along with it (**der**, **die**, **das**), the article changes shape as soon as the noun becomes the object of an action (**Akkusativ**), some verbs split in two and send half of themselves to the end of the sentence (*ich **stehe** um sechs **auf***), and the verb insists on sitting in second place, no matter what comes first.

This course tackles those four points one at a time, never all at once. Each unit starts from a conversation you can use right away — ordering coffee, saying your age, asking for directions — and only then explains why the sentence looks the way it does. The explanations are deliberately short. What is long is not the theory but the practice.

The twenty short units inside cover all the material of **Level A1 (CEFR)** — the same material as the *Start Deutsch 1* / *Goethe-Zertifikat A1* exam: introductions, where you're from, family, numbers, time, daily routine, shopping, where you live, directions, eating out, the weather, and telling what happened yesterday with the *Perfekt*.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours chopped into pieces. Language sticks through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.
Read out loud. German is pronounced far more regularly than English — once you know the reading rules, there are almost no surprises left.
Learn nouns **together with their article**. Not *Tisch*, but *der Tisch*. It's a small habit that saves months of confusion later on.

blocks.text: One thing no book can replace: someone to talk to. Use this course to get the material ready, then look for chances to use it with real people.
Enjoy the journey. *Viel Erfolg!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the German out loud without looking at the translation. Let your ears do the work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most often, yet it is where you see how German *thinks*. Example: *Wie geht es dir?* literally means "how goes it to-you?", not "how are you".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever just felt strange.
**Grammar box** — one rule per unit, with its table. Don't memorize it cold; come back to it while you do the exercises.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, each with its pronunciation. Nouns always come with their *der / die / das*.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From Unit 8 on, set aside five minutes at the start of each session to reread the dialogue from seven units back — Unit 8 reviews Unit 1, Unit 9 reviews Unit 2, and so on.
This time, read it differently: cover the German, look only at the English translation, and try to rebuild the German sentences from memory.
It feels easy, and it should. The point is not to add new material, but to move old material from "I've read that" to "it comes out on its own".

blocks.text: A word about capital letters: in German **every noun is capitalized**, wherever it stands — *der Tisch*, *ein Buch*, *meine Mutter*. It isn't a typo, and copying it from day one will save you a lot of corrections later.

The good news: German is read **almost exactly as it is written**. Unlike English, a letter sounds nearly the same in every word. Once you've mastered the short list on this page, you can read German words you have never seen before.

The "Pronunciation" column throughout this course uses English-style spelling: *ah* as in *father*, *ay* as in *say*, *eh* as in *bed*, *ee* as in *see*, *oh* as in *go*, *oo* as in *food*, *eye* as in *eye* (*nein* = neyen), *oy* as in *boy*, *ow* as in *cow*, *kh* for the throaty or hissing *ch*, and *uh* for the soft final *-er*. An unstressed final *-e* is written *e* and sounds like the *a* in *sofa*. The syllable **WRITTEN IN CAPITALS** is the stressed one. Example: *Guten Tag* = GOO-ten TAHK, *Wie geht's?* = vee GAYTS.

blocks.title: Two habits that help from day one
items: **Consonants at the end of a word go voiceless.** *und* sounds like "oont", *Tag* like "tahk", *halb* like "hahlp". The letters b, d, g at the end harden into p, t, k.

**The stress is almost always on the first syllable** — *ARbeiten*, *DEUTSCHland*, *FREUNdin*. The exceptions are borrowed words (*StuDENT*, *ResTAUrant*) and words starting with *ver-*, *be-*, *ge-*, *er-*, which are never stressed (*verSTEhen*, *beSUchen*).

blocks.text: If you're unsure about a word, read it letter by letter, just as it is. Nine times out of ten, that's already right.
These pages contain nothing new. Everything here has already appeared in the units; it is simply gathered in one place so you can glance at it while you do the exercises.
1. Verbs: the present tense (Präsens)

Vowel-changing verbs change only in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: *sprechen* → du spr**i**chst, er spr**i**cht; *fahren* → du f**ä**hrst, er f**ä**hrt; *lesen* → du l**ie**st, er l**ie**st; *nehmen* → du n**imm**st, er n**imm**t.
2. Articles
Notice the only box that really changes in the Akkusativ: the **masculine**. Everything else is exactly the same as the Nominativ. That's why the Akkusativ is far easier than it looks.
3. Possessives
4. Word order

items: **Statements:** the verb is always in **second place**. *Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin.* / *Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin.* When something else moves to the front, the subject steps behind the verb — the verb itself never moves aside.
**Yes/no questions:** the verb goes **first**. *Kommst du aus Indonesien?*
**Question-word questions:** question word, then verb. *Woher kommst du?*
**Commands:** the verb goes first. *Geh nach links!* / *Gehen Sie nach links!*

**The sentence bracket (Satzklammer):** when the verb has two parts, one sits in second place and the other is sent to the **end of the sentence**. *Ich **muss** heute lange **arbeiten**.* / *Ich **stehe** um sechs Uhr **auf**.* / *Ich **habe** Pizza **gegessen**.*
**Clauses with *weil* / *dass*:** the verb moves to the end. *Ich bleibe zu Hause, **weil** ich krank **bin**.*

blocks.text: 5. The most common prepositions

head: Always Dativ
Always Akkusativ
Dativ for location, Akkusativ for movement
rows: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu
in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen

blocks.text: Contractions to learn as whole words: *zu dem* → **zum**, *zu der* → **zur**, *in dem* → **im**, *an dem* → **am**, *in das* → **ins**, *bei dem* → **beim**.
6. Time
⚠️ *morgen* (lowercase) = tomorrow; *der Morgen* (capitalized) = morning. *Morgen früh* = tomorrow morning.
7. The everyday past (Perfekt)

**haben / sein + Partizip II at the end of the sentence.** Most verbs use *haben*. The ones that use *sein* are verbs of **movement from place to place** (*gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen*) and **change of state** (*aufstehen, einschlafen*), plus *sein* and *bleiben* themselves.
8. Numbers

The ones come **before** the tens: *einundzwanzig* = "one-and-twenty" = 21 (like the old English *four-and-twenty blackbirds*). This habit continues all the way to 99, and it is the number-one reason beginners mishear phone numbers.

This list is deliberately limited to the verbs that actually appear in this course. The third column gives the *du*/*er* forms when the vowel changes; the fourth gives the full Perfekt form with its helping verb.
The most economical way to learn them: learn **all three forms in one breath** — *fahren, fährt, ist gefahren*. Learning them separately means learning them three times.

If you've reached this page after doing all the exercises, your level is now roughly **CEFR A1**: you can introduce yourself, handle simple everyday needs, and talk briefly about yesterday and tomorrow — as long as the other person speaks slowly and is willing to repeat.
Three most useful things to do this week

items: **Go through all the dialogues once more, back to front.** Unit 20 first, Unit 1 last. Reverse order forces your brain to read the content instead of remembering the sequence.
**Write ten sentences about your own day** using the *Perfekt*. Not example sentences from the book — sentences about your life, with the names of places you actually went to.
**Find someone to talk to.** A Linguo private class, a classmate, or anyone willing to resist switching to English.

blocks.text: What's waiting at A2

items: **The Dativ in full** — not just after place prepositions, but also for the recipient: *Ich gebe **meinem Bruder** das Buch.*
**Adjectives that change too** (*ein **kleines** Haus*, *die **neue** Wohnung*) — the chapter beginners fear most, and really just one table.
**The Präteritum** for written storytelling: *war*, *hatte*, *ging*, *machte*.
**Longer subordinate clauses**: *wenn*, *dass*, *obwohl*, plus the verb that always gets sent to the end.
**Konjunktiv II for politeness**: *Ich hätte gern…*, *Könnten Sie bitte…* — two phrases that instantly make your German sound better.

blocks.text: If your goal is an official exam, your next target is the **Goethe-Zertifikat A2** or **telc Deutsch A2**. The format is the same: listening, reading, writing, speaking — and the speaking part is much shorter than people imagine.
*Alles Gute und viel Erfolg!*
